title: Kalki
tomorrow: the Bhagavata forecasts Kalki's age. why does it sound like today?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha in some lists of ten and not others: ten is a frame, not a fence, and the lake never empties. Today, the last name in every one of those lists.
screen: `TEN IS A FRAME, NOT A FENCE.`

segments.voice: Weather apps, countdowns to graduation, a tracking number that says out for delivery: a lot of life is lived toward something that hasn't happened yet. Read the Bhagavata's verses on Vishnu's forms and the grammar runs in the past. The fish came. Rama came. Krishna came, and left. Then the last name, and the verbs change. He will be born. He will ride. He will set things right. One name in the whole series is still written as will be, and it's Kalki.
screen: `OUT FOR DELIVERY.` → `THE FISH CAME. KRISHNA CAME.` → `KALKI: WILL BE.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Bhagavata says. At the twilight of the age, when those who rule have become little better than robbers, the Lord will be born as Kalki, in the village of Shambhala, in the house of a Brahmin named Vishnuyasha. He'll mount a swift horse named Devadatta, sword in hand, ride across the earth, and put down the robbers who rule as kings. Readers hold this in more than one way, so let two of them speak. One reads it straight: this is an event still ahead. The Purana says will be, and it gives a village, a father's name, a horse's name. Texts that name the horse, this reader says, aren't speaking in riddles, and waiting for Kalki is part of living in this age. Another reader listens for what the promise does right now. The dark age already has a name waiting at its close, so the dark isn't the last word. On this reading, Kalki is the age's horizon, and the point is the hope more than the date. Notice what the two share. Neither throws the verses away. Both hear the list of descents as open, its last line still unwritten. Where they part is whether the horse is coming down a road, or standing at the edge of every hard day.
screen: `EVERY OTHER NAME: CAME.` · `KALKI: WILL BE.` · `ONE READING: STILL AHEAD.` · `ANOTHER: THE AGE HAS AN END.` · then, large: `THE LAST LINE IS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Pick one hope of yours that hasn't arrived yet. Breathe in and name the wish; breathe out and name what stands in its way; on the next breath, name one small step that's yours to take. Then rest with that step for the rest of the sit.
Kalki: the form of Vishnu the Bhagavata says will be born at the twilight of the age, in Shambhala, riding a swift horse.
For the road: Kalki, the one name in the series still written as will be. Day fifteen sixty-four, done.

howItsDone: Hindus hold the Kalki verses in more than one way: some speak of Kalki as still to come, and others read the promise as a sign that the dark age has an end.

fork.setup: Sam reads Kalki as pure symbol and asks you to make the best case for 'an event still ahead.' what's strongest?

fork.reveal: a fair case stands on the text: bhavishyati, Shambhala, Vishnuyasha, Devadatta. Details like those are why some readers wait for an event.

chat.meaning: The Bhagavata writes Kalki in the future tense. Some read an event still ahead; some hear a promise that the hard age has an end.

Kalki.meaning: the form of Vishnu still to come

Shambhala.meaning: the village where the Bhagavata says Kalki will be born

Devadatta.meaning: Kalki's swift horse in the Bhagavata

Vishnuyasha.meaning: the Brahmin in whose house Kalki will be born

Brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.3.25 (Kalki, son of Vishnuyasha, at the twilight of the age, when rulers are like robbers)
Bhagavata Purana 12.2.18–20 (born in Shambhala in Vishnuyasha's house; the horse Devadatta; the sword; the robbers who rule as kings)

notes: Kalki run, day 1 of 3 (1564–1566). Angle: the future tense, as a debate between two readings (an event still ahead; a promise that the dark age ends). Both are given voice; neither is ranked. 1565 takes the Kali age he comes into; 1566 what comes after, and closes the Puranas part.

Paraphrase of Bhagavata 1.3.25 and 12.2.18–20. The text's violence (killing robber-kings in large numbers) is softened to 'put down the robbers who rule as kings'; Keeper to confirm that's fair. No horse color given (popular images show white; the verses used here name the horse, not its color).
'bhavishyati' is the verb in 1.3.25 (bhavishyati) and 12.2.18 (pradurbhavishyati); confirm the simplified form is fair.

The two readings are put as 'one reader / another reader'; confirm both are fair to living Hindu views, and that 'the point is the hope more than the date' is not pressed on those who expect an event.
